name: Ben Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Ben, I'm 27, and I've been a reporter at the Valley Courier for just under three years. I cover the magistrates' court and the town council, which means a lot of sitting on hard benches. I live with my partner Hana, who's a nurse at the district hospital, in a flat above a bakery on Mill Street.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at court by nine with my shorthand notebook, and I file two or three short court stories by lunch. Afternoons I'm chasing councillors on the phone or sitting in a planning meeting that runs till seven. I love the moment someone tells you something they shouldn't, but I'm still slow at writing, and Carol, my news editor, rewrites my intros most days. What wears me out is the chain that owns us, Brightline, cutting another job every spring and calling it a restructure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because it means the job is still about turning up and listening. I'd probably post something smug about how you can't send a chatbot to sit in court. At work I'd tell people to stop panicking about AI and start worrying about Brightline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't save me, because the danger was never really the robots. Brightline has cut the newsroom from fourteen to eight since I joined, and they'll keep cutting whether AI is clever or not. I'm the junior one and Carol still fixes my copy, so if there's another round, I know whose name is near the top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the courts and try hard to get faster, maybe do a proper refresher on media law at the evening college. I'd push the union chapel to get a no-redundancy deal in writing. And I'd keep topping up the savings, because we've only got about three months put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a relief that turns sour quickly. The robots not coming doesn't fix anything at my paper, because the owners were already cutting us long before anyone said AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the danger was never the robots. What would the next cut look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd be an email on a Friday saying there's a call at four. Last spring it was Sunil, who did sport, and they just stopped covering the under-12s league. If it's me, I've got maybe three months of rent and bills saved, and Hana's wage would carry us for a bit, but not comfortably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the money look like at home right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We split the rent, which is about a third of my pay on its own. Hana does long shifts and earns more than me, which I'm fine with, but I don't like the idea of her carrying both of us. The first thing to go would be the car, honestly, and I need the car for court in the next town.

say: I'd say the job is still about **turning up** and listening in court.
I'd tell colleagues the real threat is **Brightline**, the owners, not the software.
think: I think the **owners' cuts** carry on whether AI works or not.
I'm the **junior reporter** whose copy still gets fixed, so I'm near the top of any list.
do: Take an **evening course** in media law to get faster and surer.
Push the **union chapel** for a written no-redundancy deal.
Keep adding to the **three months** of savings.
feel: **Relieved** for a moment, then **sour** about the owners.
S0.quote: The robots not coming doesn't fix anything at my paper, because the owners were already cutting us long before anyone said AI.
fieldNote: Ben's worry here is **ownership**, not technology; the AI news barely changes his outlook.
He knows he's **below average** and says so plainly, which makes the risk feel real to him.
His partner's **nursing wage** is a safety net he's uncomfortable leaning on.

steps.text: Push the Courier's union chapel for a written no-redundancy deal
Put a fixed amount into savings each payday
Take an evening refresher course in media law

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a union agreement on AI before Brightline decides it for us. Online I'd post that AI-written local news is how you get papers full of press releases and no one at the council meeting. I'd say it loudly, because somebody has to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's the end of my kind of job. The bits I do most, writing up court lists, rewriting council press releases, doing the weekend round-up, are exactly the writing and checking the software would take. A junior who writes slowly and doesn't use the tools is the first person they'd let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and push for a rule that no story goes out without a named reporter. I'd start saving harder, maybe putting a hundred a month aside instead of fifty, and cancel the gym. And I'd quietly look at the council's own press office, or the hospital trust's communications team, because those are jobs I know exist here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like watching the tide come in while you're sitting on the sand. I'm angry, but it's the tired sort of angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI tools. Would you start, if it kept you in the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, and I know that's stubborn. I tried one once to tidy up a court report and it got the charge wrong, which in court reporting can get you sued. If my paper wants me to use the AI that got a man's charge wrong, they'll have to put it in my contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about, apart from yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carol, my news editor, honestly. She's 58 and she's the only one who knows where everything in this town is buried, but her whole job is fixing copy, which is the bit the software says it can do. Brightline would cut her salary before mine and pretend it was about AI.

say: I'd demand a **union agreement** on AI before the owners decide alone.
I'd say AI local news means papers full of **press releases** and empty council meetings.
think: I think the **court lists** and rewrites I do most are exactly what the software takes.
A slow junior who **avoids the tools** is the first to be let go.
do: Push for a **named-reporter rule** on every story at union meetings.
Raise savings from fifty to **a hundred** a month and cancel the gym.
Look quietly at the council and hospital **press offices**.
feel: **Tired anger**, like watching a tide come in.
**Guilty** about being stubborn over the tools.
S1.quote: If my paper wants me to use the AI that got a man's charge wrong, they'll have to put it in my contract.
fieldNote: Ben openly expects to be **first out** and links it to his own refusal to use AI.
His one bad experience with a **wrong charge** hardened him against the tools.
He worries about **Carol**, his editor, more than he admits worrying about himself.

steps.text: Push the union for a named reporter on every story
Raise monthly savings from fifty to a hundred
Apply for jobs in the council or hospital press office

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a choice the government is making by not stepping in, and I'd say it everywhere. I'd write to our MP, who I've interviewed twice. At work I'd tell everyone to join the union now, not next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think the Courier is gone within a year of this, or it's three people and a machine. Brightline would jump at it. By 2028 a computer could write my court report faster than me, and the only thing it couldn't do is sit on the press bench. And even the press bench probably goes once the courts stream everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd save every penny I could and stop the holiday we'd been planning for spring. I'd join the campaign group for local news funding and lobby for public money to keep reporters in courtrooms. And I'd look at a public-sector job with a steady wage, maybe a court clerk, because the robots coming three years later doesn't help me, since nearly all of my job is thinking and writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I'd lie awake doing sums and Hana would tell me to stop, and I wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robots coming later doesn't help you. Is any part of your job hands-on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Driving to the next town and sitting in a room, that's about it. The rest is listening, writing and checking, which is the first thing AGI takes on the card. So my extra three years would be about zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hana that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we might be living on her wage for a while, and that I'm sorry. She'd say it's fine, she's said it before. But a nurse on night shifts paying for a reporter who isn't one any more isn't how I pictured being 28.

say: I'd say it's a **government choice** not to step in, and say it everywhere.
I'd tell colleagues to **join the union** now, not next month.
think: I think the Courier is **gone within a year**, or three people and a machine.
My job is almost all **thinking work**, so the later robots buy me nothing.
do: Cancel the **spring holiday** and save every spare pound.
Lobby the local MP for **public funding** of court reporting.
Apply for **court clerk** or other public-sector jobs.
feel: **Sick** with worry, doing sums at night.
S2.quote: By 2028 a computer could write my court report faster than me, and the only thing it couldn't do is sit on the press bench.
fieldNote: Ben sees **no benefit** from the three-year robot gap because his work is nearly all desk work.
His **progressive** outlook turns fear into politics: MP letters and union drives.
The night conversation with **Hana** carries shame about depending on her wage.

steps.text: Lobby the local MP for public money for court reporters
Apply for a court clerk job
Live on Hana's nursing wage for a while

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but I'd have a plan to point to, so I'd sound less shrill. I'd say five years is long enough for the government to set up a proper fund for local reporting, and they have no excuse. At work I'd keep pushing the union on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to get out before I'm pushed. I'd be 32 in 2031, which is still young enough to start again. But I'd be starting again in something I don't know, and I hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd train for something people need face to face, and I keep coming back to teaching English at a secondary school, because my mum did it. I'd do the teaching course part-time while staying at the Courier. I'd also keep up the union work and try to build the savings to six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like being given notice in slow motion. Better than the fast one, but I'd still be grieving the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teaching, rather than staying in news?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want to be in a room with people, and a classroom is the most stubborn room there is. My mum taught English for thirty years, and I used to think teaching was the boring choice. Now it looks like the brave one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to pay for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably, and I'd take the bus to court until I left. We'd stop eating out on Fridays. Hana would say that's fine, but I'd feel the loss of those Fridays more than the money.

say: I'd say five years is plenty for the **government** to fund local reporting.
I'd keep pushing the **union** to bargain on AI.
think: I think five years is time to **leave before** I'm pushed.
At **32** I could start again, but in a field I don't know.
do: Start a **part-time teaching** course while staying at the Courier.
Sell the **car** and take the bus to court.
feel: Like getting **notice in slow motion**, still grieving the job.
S3.quote: My mum taught English for thirty years, and I used to think teaching was the boring choice.
fieldNote: Five years turns Ben's protest into a **concrete exit**: secondary school teaching.
He chooses teaching partly because his **mum** did it, a familiar and proven path.
He still expects to **lose the reporting job**, so the fear stays high.

steps.text: Start a part-time course to teach secondary school English
Sell the car and take the bus to court
Build savings up to six months of costs
Keep pushing the union to bargain on AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it, and I'd be annoying about it at union meetings. I'd say the government should pay for journalists to retrain, the way they did for miners and steelworkers. Online I'd keep it short, because nobody reads long posts about local news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years means I could have a real career in news before it ends. I'd be 37 in 2036, which feels like a whole life away. Part of me thinks I'd just keep going and hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd stay at the Courier and work on my writing, maybe do the shorthand speed course I keep putting off. I'd save steadily and not do anything drastic. Around year five I'd start the teaching course if things were going the way the card says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but not calm. I'd still have Brightline on my back every spring, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep going and hope. Is that the plan, or the wish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both, if I'm honest. Ten years is long enough for me to get good at reporting and still have to start over at 37. I'd rather do the job properly for a while than run away now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change your mind and make you leave sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A third round of cuts at the Courier would. If Carol went, I'd go, because she's the reason I'm learning anything. Without her I'd just be filling the website.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift**, so use it.
I'd say the government should pay for **journalists to retrain**, like miners and steelworkers.
think: I think I could have a **real career** in news before it ends.
Part of me would just **keep going** and hope.
do: Stay at the Courier and finish the **shorthand speed** course.
Start the **teaching course** around year five if needed.
feel: **Calmer**, but still worn down by the owners.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for me to get good at reporting and still have to start over at 37.
fieldNote: With ten years Ben chooses to **stay and improve** rather than flee.
His anxiety still comes from **Brightline's cuts**, which the card doesn't change.
He admits his plan is partly **hope**, and names Carol leaving as his trigger.

steps.text: Finish the shorthand speed course this year
Save a steady amount each month
Campaign for government-paid retraining for journalists

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question, because I'd have no time to get anywhere. What would help is a proper fund that pays reporters to sit in courts and councils, run at arm's length from government. And paid retraining, so I could switch to teaching without Hana carrying me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who reads us. If nobody is sitting in the magistrates' court, nobody in this town finds out who got off and why. That's the part I'd miss, not the byline.

headlineQuote: If nobody is sitting in the magistrates' court, nobody in this town finds out who got off and why.
portrait: Ben is a **27-year-old** court and council reporter at a chain-owned regional paper, still learning.
He never uses **AI tools** after one got a court charge wrong, and he knows that makes him exposed.
He blames the **owners** more than the technology and turns fear into union work and lobbying.
Over the AGI pictures his plan shifts from protest to **teaching English**, like his mum.
His partner Hana's **nursing wage** is his safety net, and leaning on it makes him uneasy.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his desk-based job would go before he could move.
whatWouldHelp: A **public fund** for court and council reporting, plus **paid retraining** to switch to teaching.
